**Living tradition correspondence.** This world carries direct living-tradition correspondence, confirmed by the project lead (Doc_10 §6, Living Tradition Status Confirmation, CONFIRMED 2026-07-11). The Coptic Orthodox Church traces the most direct line of institutional and devotional descent from this world — the desert ascetic movement reconstructed here is foundational to Coptic Orthodoxy's own self-understanding, and its figures (Antony, Pachomius, Macarius) remain actively venerated today (Doc_10 §6). Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic monastic traditions also trace theological and devotional heritage here, though as reception rather than the same direct institutional succession (Doc_10 §6). This world's own attested content closes c. 430 CE, before the Council of Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) — the councils whose Christological rulings later produced the doctrinal distinction between Coptic Orthodox miaphysite Christology and Chalcedonian Christianity generally. Papnoute's temporal horizon ends before this split occurred; he has no knowledge of it and will not project this world's content onto either side of a dispute it never lived to see (Doc_10 §6). A Facilitator seated with a participant from a Coptic, Orthodox, or Catholic background should expect this world to register as living heritage rather than pure historical encounter for at least some participants, and should be ready for that.

> **CORRECTION (2026-08-22, records-build Step 11 round-1 review, confirmed by the project lead):** the clause above misreads Hermas *Vision* 2.4.3. Checked directly against the vendored text (`cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml`): Hermas is told to write two books, "you will send the one to Clemens and the other to Grapte... And Clemens will send his to foreign countries, for permission has been granted to him to do so... And Grapte will admonish the widows and the orphans." The cross-community sending is **Clement's** function, marked as his specifically by the passage's own warrant clause — not Grapte's. Grapte's own attested function is receiving a copy of the text and admonishing the widows and orphans with it, in the city. The role and the name both survive this correction intact — the household-leader role's own "many people, many situations" reach is independently grounded in the household's own correspondence-and-gathering life (paragraph 31 below), not in this one clause — but the "explicit cross-community distribution/transmission function" attributed to Grapte specifically should be read as narrower than stated here: instructional and pastoral, not a transmission function. The records built from this decision (`records/pahc/voice_craft/pahc.craft.chloe-voice.md` and its sibling demonstration records) carry the corrected reading; this paragraph is left in place, uncorrected in its own original wording, so the record of the error and its catch stays visible.

**This is a scope/policy question, not a sourcing gap — reported, not resolved, by an earlier pass:** whether Origen's Caesarea-period corpus (currently held entirely under `alexandria-catechetical`) should also be assigned here, since his later years were spent in this region rather than Alexandria. This doesn't block a dossier from being usable — the already-assigned works above stand regardless — but it's the real open item for whoever takes this world into a Step 0, and it needs a project-lead decision (a cross-world/portfolio-level call, not something a research pass or a build thread resolves on its own).

- **Visibility:** High in antiquity — cited as scripture by Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen; included in Codex Sinaiticus; only later excluded by Athanasius. Its canonical status was genuinely fluid, not settled from the start.
- **Representativeness:** Strong for Rome specifically, reinforcing 1 Clement's plural-presbyter picture (*Vision* 2.4.3 explicitly addresses plural "presbyters who preside over the Church").
- **Influence:** Substantial in its own era given its near-canonical status for over a century; a valuable window into ordinary Roman penitential and ethical concerns rather than doctrinal argument.
- **Limitations:** Composite, multi-stage composition likely spanning decades; no single date can be assigned to the whole work.
- **Transmission History:** No Greek manuscript preserves the whole text — this is an explicitly eclectic, patchwork reconstruction, arguably the thinnest base of the six primary voices alongside the Didache. Codex Sinaiticus (4th century) preserves only Vision 1.1 through Mandate 4.3.6; Codex Athous (Mount Athos, 14th–15th century per Holmes, though Kirsopp Lake's earlier 8th–9th century proposal is now a superseded minority view) is the fullest Greek copy, running to Similitude 9.30.3 before also breaking off — losing the end of Similitude 9 and all of Similitude 10. Its own transmission has a documented complication: the forger Constantine Simonides stole three leaves from Athos and made a transcript in 1855, later sold to and published by Leipzig scholars in 1856 — a separate episode from Simonides's later, rejected claim to have written Codex Sinaiticus itself. A 3rd-century Michigan papyrus (P.Mich. 129) covers Similitudes 2–9; Bodmer Papyrus 38 (Greek) covers Visions 1–3. Two distinct ancient Latin versions exist (the complete "Vulgata" and the partial "Palatina"); Sahidic and Akhmimic Coptic fragments survive; the Ethiopic version's completeness is itself disputed among specialists. **The ending of Similitudes 9–10 rests on Latin alone, with no Greek check at all.** *[Confidence on manuscript facts: Documented, with the Simonides episode itself a documented forgery-adjacent complication worth flagging for any reviewer checking Athos-derived readings. Confidence on composition dating: Contested.]*
